chain.g: allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith

ety.text: From Late Middle English fidelite (“allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith”), from Old French fidélité (“faithfulness, fidelity”) (modern French fidélité), from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness, fidelity”), from fidēlis (“dependable, trustworthy; faithful, loyal”) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns denoting a state of being).

senses.d: Often followed by to or towards: faithfulness or loyalty towards a person, a group, one's civic or moral duties, etc.; allegiance; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: the fidelity of the civil servants to their country

senses.d: Faithfulness or loyalty to one's partner or spouse, including restraint from romantic or sexual relationships with third parties.
Faithfulness to God and one's religion.
Accuracy, or exact correspondence, to some given fact or quality; exactness.
The closeness of association between an organism and a plant community.
Chiefly in high fidelity, low fidelity, etc.: the degree to which a system accurately reproduces an input such as an image or sound.
In by one's fidelity, to break fidelity, to give fidelity, etc.: one's pledge or promise to act in good faith; an oath, a word of honour.
ex: By my fidelity this is not vvell.

senses.d: Of a person: honesty, trustworthiness; (countable) an instance of this.
ex: [O]ure lord Jeſus hymſelfe dooth tetifye vnto vs that we receiue hys body and blood. Ought we to doubte of his fidelitie and testimony?
